title: The Borrowed Autopsy
premise: Jonah Vasquez, the coroner of salt-bitten Cape Verity, receives a letter confessing to a thirty-year-old drowning he ruled an accident at the start of his career, followed by a second letter promising another death unless Jonah finally tells the truth about what he saw that night. As the tide surrenders old bones and old lies, Jonah discovers the confessor is someone whose life he quietly saved by falsifying that first report, and that the town's beloved founding families buried the victim together. In the end, Jonah must choose between protecting the living who depend on his silence and giving the drowned their name back, and he chooses truth, testifying at a cost that strips him of his office but returns him to himself.
about_author: Gideon Marchetti is a former coastal paramedic who spent a decade writing incident reports before turning to fiction. He lives in a rented house above a bait shop, where he claims the fog does half his editing.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes, One Hand
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Between routine cases, Jonah opens twin letters: a confession to the 1994 drowning of a boy he ruled accidental, and a threat promising a second death if he stays silent. Handwriting analysis suggests both were written by the same person, decades apart. The beat is dread arriving in an ordinary morning, the past refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: The Grave I Named
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, with a flashback to 1994. He revisits his first autopsy, the pressure from the Hollis family, and the small falsification he made that let a terrified teenager walk free. He realizes the confession writer knows details only someone at the scene could know. The beat is guilt resurfacing as a professional wound he can't chart away.

chapters.title: What the Tide Keeps
chapters.summary: Deputy Marisol Okafor's POV. A storm uncovers bones on the flats near the old Hollis boathouse, and Marisol, who idolizes Jonah, notices his reaction to the site. She begins pulling the 1994 file quietly. The beat is loyalty forming a crack, as admiration curdles into suspicion she doesn't yet want to name.

chapters.title: The Alibi Season
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He interviews the surviving Hollis siblings, now pillars of the town, and finds their thirty-year-old alibis rehearsed to the syllable, word-for-word identical. One sibling, Ada, nearly breaks and warns him to let the water keep what it took. The beat is the vertigo of realizing an entire town agreed on a story.

chapters.title: A Second Body, Promised
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The threatened second death arrives: Ada Hollis found drowned, staged exactly like 1994. Marisol must tell Jonah, and watches him recognize the staging before anyone announces it. The beat is horror sharpening into certainty that Jonah is either the killer's target, confessor, or accomplice, and Marisol can no longer look away.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Walked Home
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He tracks down Danny Reyes, the teenager he saved with his falsified report, now a quiet carpenter with a family. Danny confesses he wrote both letters, but insists he didn't kill Ada; he only wanted Jonah to finally say out loud what they both did. The beat is the collapse of Jonah's assumption that the confessor is his enemy.

chapters.title: Thirty Years of Quiet
chapters.summary: Alternating Jonah and Marisol POV. Marisol confronts Jonah with the file discrepancies, and he gives her the whole truth: the Hollis patriarch killed the boy, the family covered it, and Jonah's mercy buried it deeper. Marisol must decide whether the man she trusted is a witness or a suspect. The beat is loyalty and truth tearing in opposite directions.

chapters.title: The Founders' Ledger
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Digging through the Hollis estate papers, Jonah finds the ledger proving the family paid off the coroner before him, meaning falsified reports are the town's inheritance, not his invention alone. The surviving Hollis brother offers him money and silence one last time. The beat is the seduction of complicity offered as respectability, and its refusal.

chapters.title: What the Water Gave Back
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, climax. Lured to the flats by a final letter, Jonah faces the true killer of 1994, the patriarch's son, who has killed Ada to keep the pattern unbroken and now needs Jonah gone too. Danny arrives, and Marisol's sirens cut through the fog. The beat is the past made physical: a struggle in the shallows where the first body fell.

chapters.title: Every Grave by Name
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, resolution. The killer is arrested; the drowned boy's real name is read aloud at a reburial Jonah officiates, having surrendered his office rather than sign one more softened report. Danny stands at the edge of the crowd, forgiven but not absolved. The beat is the price of survival paid in full, and a man made visible at last, to his town and to himself.
